extracted.intended_audience: GNM (Guardian News & Media) journalists, editors and freelance contributors
extracted.subtask_description: Internal editorial code and legal/professional guidance for journalists working for Guardian News & Media, covering privacy, verification, legal compliance, professional conduct, conflicts of interest, sourcing and other newsroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography and video footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken when taking photographs or filming in both public and private places in circumstances where an individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy, is unaware that the picture or footage is being taken for publication, and/or has not provided consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The location and the activity engaged in are important considerations. Clause 2 does not prohibit the use of long-lens photography, but the use of a long lens may be a relevant factor when considering whether there has been an intrusion into an individual’s privacy in a particular situation. See editorial code guidance section P on pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying details
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution about reporting and publishing identifying details that may enable others to intrude on privacy or safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing street names, house numbers or other identifying details that could facilitate intrusion upon people who have become the subject of media coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the Omand principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proportionality before committing actions that infringe privacy: degree of intrusion must be justified by seriousness of story and public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should ask five questions: (1) Is there sufficient cause? (2) Is there integrity of motive? (3) Will the methods used be in proportion to the seriousness of the story? (4) Is there proper authority? (5) Is there a reasonable prospect of success? Where there is a legitimate expectation of privacy, be able to demonstrate why an infringement is justified in the public interest. Consult senior duty editor and editorial legal when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every effort to contact the person or organisation that is the subject of a story before publication to put allegations to them and give opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assists accuracy and fairness and is vital in demonstrating that the public interest in publishing has been considered. Take account of complexity, time zones; more serious allegations increase obligation to allow response. Editorial legal services can advise on best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources — anonymity and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: When a source seeks anonymity or requests confidentiality, discuss the request with the relevant senior duty editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists have a moral obligation to protect confidential sources. Otherwise, sources should be identified as specifically as possible. See clause 14 of the editorial code and guidance on anonymous contributions and source care/protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing — social media material
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM’s editorial code covers content published on social media; material from social media must be considered as with any other source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before accessing, publishing or sharing material taken from social media or the wider internet, consider legal, copyright and ethical issues. Familiarise with GNM social media guidelines and section Q professional behaviour guidance on social media conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subterfuge and covert behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should identify themselves as GNM employees when gathering material; subterfuge is a rare exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any use of subterfuge must be approved in advance by the relevant senior duty editor and editorial legal consulted. Applies to hidden cameras/listening/recording devices and material acquired by subterfuge, even if not published. If GNM is offered such material by third parties, seek advice from the managing editor and editorial legal. See clause 10 on clandestine devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting suicide and self-harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise particular care with stories about suicide and self-harm, bearing in mind the risk of encouraging others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with presentation, pictures and descriptions of methods — refer to methods in general terms where possible; avoid speculation about single motives; avoid trigger images (places where suicides occurred, scars); consider relatives’ feelings. Be careful in reporting legal proceedings and inquests and usually avoid publishing every detail revealed. Where appropriate append helpline notes (Samaritans, US Lifeline, crisis text services) and follow Samaritans’ media guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be tenacious in seeking reliable corroboration; particularly careful verifying online, social media and email sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State level of substantiation when relevant (eg “the Guardian has been unable to independently verify the facts”). Do not state as fact information from someone you cannot authenticate — use qualifying phrasing. Be open with readers about medium used for interviews (eg email, Zoom). Desk editors as well as reporters are responsible for satisfaction with sources; subeditors should challenge dependability of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal compliance responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should familiarise themselves with laws that may affect reporting and consult editorial legal team when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws include defamation, privacy, data protection, copyright, contempt, national security, official secrets and terrorism. As a global organisation we can be sued anywhere. Journalists should (a) familiarise with current law and undertake in-house training, (b) consult in-house or external legal departments/night lawyers in a timely manner before publication about specific concerns, (c) read regular legal notices about active cases/reporting restrictions, (d) complete online legal training when requested, (e) discuss intentions with editor-in-chief or managing editor if considering giving evidence to any court. On public interest matters also refer to editorial code and professional behaviour sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery Act 2010 — payments and hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware the Bribery Act creates offences including offering/accepting bribery and bribing foreign public officials; hospitality/facilitation payments can fall within the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should familiarise themselves with GNM anti-bribery and corruption, and gifts and hospitality policies. There is no public interest defence; in extreme cases duress may be a defence. Discuss beforehand with senior duty editor if concerned payments might fall into these categories and inform the relevant senior duty editor afterwards if payments are requested or made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt of court and court reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles relating to ongoing court cases can prejudice proceedings; statutory restrictions exist from arrest until trial/appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn off online comments on such stories; be particularly wary of reporting on cases involving juries, inquests, family courts, children, vulnerable adults and sexual offence victims. Check for court orders restricting reporting. Contemporaneous, fair and accurate open-court reports generally provide a defence against defamation and contempt, but publishing invasive or graphic details may still harm dignity or privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use content (pictures, text or other media) without checking that GNM has necessary permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissions include agency material and social media content. Check with picture desk, relevant senior duty editor or editorial legal before using material without permission. Limited legal exceptions may exist but must be confirmed. Familiarise with GNM social media guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data protection and the journalism exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal data is widely defined; journalistic uses often rely on GNM legal bases or the journalism exemption under UK GDPR/DPA 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use the exemption, processing must be for journalism with view to publication and a reasonable belief publication is in the public interest, and that complying with usual GDPR/DPA requirements would be incompatible with journalism. Special category data and data about suspected offenders are treated more onerously. For high-profile/intrusive stories, keep contemporaneous evidence of decision-making and consult senior duty editor and editorial legal. Always keep personal data secure and report data incidents promptly to InfoSec, the DPO and editorial legal. Data subject requests should be referred to editorial legal. Familiarise with ICO code of practice and attend training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation — legal test and pre-publication defence
rubrics_metrics.description: To sue for defamation, claimant must show identifiability, publication, defamation and serious harm; publisher must prove a defence (truth, honest opinion, public interest, privilege).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-publication right to reply or invitation to comment can be important to the public interest defence. Consider privacy and data protection in pre-publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy — reasonable expectation and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect people's privacy in line with Article 8 ECHR; consider whether there is a reasonable expectation of privacy and balance that against public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable expectation of privacy is fact-specific; celebrities and people in public places may still retain privacy in some circumstances. Any infringement in gathering or publication must be justifiable and proportionate. The UK Supreme Court considers those under criminal investigation or arrested to have a reasonable expectation of privacy until charged and should not generally be named — exceptions require editorial legal and senior duty editor approval. Consult senior duty editor and editorial legal when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid conflicts that could undermine editorial integrity or appear to; disclose circumstances that may appear to be conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the managing editor if in doubt. Declare personal or financial interests, relationships or activities that could create an impression of conflict on staff and freelance online biographies. See sections on corporate and personal declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial products and promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: No Guardian/Observer journalist or primary freelance contributor should personally endorse commercial products without express permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freelancers writing about a product/brand they earn money from must declare the relationship in advance and include a footnote. Journalists should not promote financial interests of interviewees or their sponsors to secure access. Promotional information should only be included where the editor judges it of genuine interest. Journalists should not be influenced by commercial considerations (advertisers, affiliate links). Editorial staff may not work on paid content produced by commercial teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioning practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Support good commissioning practice including fair treatment of freelancers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should make reference to GNM’s freelance charter when commissioning new contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct at work
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone representing GNM should behave professionally, dress appropriately and be courteous in all exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies in person, by phone, email, online or on social media. Journalists and contributors should adhere to GNM social media guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of employee personal information
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists with access to personal information relating to other GNM employees must treat such information as confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disclose such information except in the course of discharging formal responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy approval policy
rubrics_metrics.description: No one should be given the right to copy approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never offer copy approval as a method of securing interviews or cooperation. In certain circumstances people may be allowed to see quotes to confirm accuracy; exceptional cases allowing preview of copy require senior editorial approval and must not be made subject to any obligation to alter copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits and bylines
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge the source of published material obtained from another organisation; bylines only on material substantially the bylined journalist's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes taken from other newspapers and social media should be credited. If an article contains a significant amount of agency copy the agency should be credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations of corporate interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge relationships between Guardian/Observer and Guardian Media Group (GMG) where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone writing about GMG-related businesses should seek comments/confirmation in the normal way. Journalists should familiarise themselves with GMG companies and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations of personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must declare significant connections when writing about topics with which they have a connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: (1) Always declare significant connections to a head of department or editor during preparation and possibly in print/online. (2) Connections don't have to be formal—advisory roles require declaration. (3) Obvious connections that explain why a writer was asked to contribute should still be stated at end of contribution. (4) Columnists may have more latitude than staff reporters. (5) Generally do not commission/write about/quote a relative, partner or close friend; if exception made, make the connection clear. (6) Commissioning editors should ensure freelancers are aware of these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial reporting ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report objectively on financial products and do not use or pass on financial information for personal profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write about shares in which you or associates have a significant interest; do not deal in shares you have written or will write about in the near future. Distinguish clearly between comment/conjecture and fact. Business desk staff must list shares and transactions in a register which must be kept up to date. Financial journalists should not be regular market traders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freebies and gifts policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not use their position to obtain private benefit; payments/gifts must not undermine accuracy, fairness or independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report attempts to induce favourable coverage. Disclose payments/gifts where relevant. When an airline, hotel or other interest bears transport/accommodation costs, make this clear in footnotes; acceptance is conditional on GNM being free to report as it sees fit. Journalists should not be accompanied on free trips by partners/family/friends except rare exceptions cleared with managing editor; gifts over £50 should be returned or donated; items supplied for use in reviews should be returned/stored/donated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freelance work and media appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time staff journalists should not contribute to other publications or media outlets without prior authorisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff should consult the communications team before appearing on TV/other media; requests to film inside GNM offices must be sent to media.enquiries@theguardian.com for approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of GNM connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use GNM position to seek personal benefit in business, financial or commercial transactions not available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use GNM email addresses or social media accounts in connection with non-GNM matters or cite Guardian/Observer connection to resolve consumer grievances or obtain discounts/deals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers of financial assistance to subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not act as intermediaries for donations or fundraising on behalf of people featured in Guardian coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set up crowdfunders connected with Guardian/Observer articles; do not link to online fundraising appeals without approval of senior duty editor. You may put willing parties in contact, but should not act as intermediary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside interests and political involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have a right to a private life but outside interests must not conflict with professional duties or compromise editorial integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active political involvement may give rise to actual or perceived conflicts; generally not appropriate for staff to hold political office. Staff should discuss with editor-in-chief/US/Australia editor or managing editor before undertaking activities such as working for a political party, outside employment likely to conflict, giving evidence to court, making representations to official bodies about GNM material, chairing/speaking at public events. Payments for approved public speaking during work hours should not be accepted; reasonable fees for significant private-time preparation may be accepted with prior approval. Never provide PR advice. Personal/financial interests should be declared on staff and freelance biographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments for stories and use of agents
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM does not pay sources or interviewees; rare exceptions require senior duty editor approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not engage paid non-journalistic agents or assistants without prior knowledge and approval of the relevant senior duty editor. Occasional tip fees may be paid to bona fide freelance journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships and editorial involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not generally commission, write about, photograph, film or make editorial decisions about individuals with whom they have a close personal or financial relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a relationship with a public figure or journalist inside or outside GNM creates a potential conflict and discuss with the managing editor if it does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct — professionalism and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat people with respect and professionalism on social media and remember private posts can be shared publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common sense before posting. Familiarise with full social media guidelines and guidance on staying safe online, responding to abuse and where to get support. See section U and section on sourcing social media material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source care and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists working regularly with sources must understand practicalities and limitations of source protection methods and not promise outcomes beyond GNM control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend training by editorial legal and InfoSec; consult InfoSec to ensure technology/software are up to date; familiarise with secure contact methods such as Secure Drop. Electronic devices must comply with GNM encryption standards. Consider meeting in person or using post/hand delivery where appropriate. Further resources include 'Protecting Sources and Whistleblowers in a Digital Age' and related initiatives supported by GNM.
